_: Lesson settings — the situation each lesson opens on. One per lesson, in step order.
_design: lesson-setting-design-v1.md. Block order: setting → line → what → build → when → watch.
_register: LLOYD, SESSION 17: the situation should be something REQUIRED, not merely observed — the business a learner cannot avoid. Residence card, ward office, immigration, the errands of arriving. That is what a Japanese learner's life in Japan actually consists of in month one, and it is why the medicine-booklet version of ls-teikutekuru was replaced by the residence card.
_method: Step by step, in order, reading each lesson's own what/build/when/watch first so the situation fits THAT point rather than the point being bent to fit a situation. Steps 0-2 complete; the four cross-step lessons from the first proof pass are kept at the end.
_scope: STEPS 0, 1 AND 2 COMPLETE (23 lessons), plus 4 earlier proof lessons. Stopping here for Lloyd's review before Step 3 onward.
_vocab: Japanese stays inside the step's own bank plus what the module's own examples already use at that point. Step 0 has no vocabulary at all, so its lines are ILLUSTRATIVE — shown, not yet producible, which is what Step 0 is for.
_status: AI-AUTHORED, NOT REVIEWED. One batch per lesson. Three questions: are the claims true; is the line natural for THIS situation; is this the pattern a Japanese speaker would reach for here.
_exclusions: cc-* lessons already ARE situations and get no setting. b-* composition tasks are exercises, not explanations.

items.why_this_lesson: The first thing a learner does in Japan is stand at a counter and hand something over. Word order is the lesson, so the setting only has to produce one short sentence and let the shape be visible.
items.setting: The immigration hall, somewhere after the flight and before the country starts. You filled in a landing card on the plane. At the counter the officer will take your passport, and if you are staying more than three months you will walk away from that desk holding a residence card with your name on it — the document you are now legally required to carry every day you are here.

line.en: Card show. — I show the card.

items.turn: The thing being acted on comes first and the action comes last, which is the reverse of English and stays that way in every sentence you will ever build. Nothing about this is irregular — it is simply where Japanese keeps its verbs, and it is consistent enough to stop noticing within a month.
claims: Residence cards are issued to foreign nationals staying more than three months (mid-to-long-term residents)
Carrying the residence card is a legal requirement for those residents aged 16 and over
flags: STEP 0 LINE IS ILLUSTRATIVE. 見せます is not taught until later; the lesson exists to show sentence shape before any grammar, exactly as the module's own 'Coffee drink.' example does.

items.why_this_lesson: Omission needs a moment where the missing information is obviously already known. A clerk filling in your own record from your own form is the cleanest version of that: she has your name in front of her, so saying it again would be strange rather than polite.
items.setting: The ward office, second week. You are registering your address — a thing you must do within fourteen days of moving in, and the thing every other piece of paperwork will hang off. The clerk has your form, your card and your passport spread out in front of her. She looks up and asks what you do for a living, and there is exactly one piece of information missing.

line.en: Teacher. — I'm a teacher.

items.turn: Nothing is missing. Japanese stops the sentence where the information stops, and anything already shared falls away. Supplying 私は here would not be wrong so much as odd — it reads as a contrast with somebody, and there is nobody else at the counter.
claims: Address registration must be completed within 14 days of moving in
The resulting 住民票 record underpins insurance, banking and phone contracts

items.why_this_lesson: です is the shortest complete sentence in the language, so the setting should be one where you are asked to state a bare fact about yourself and nothing more. A status-of-residence question is exactly that, and it is a question with consequences.
items.setting: A police box, a Tuesday evening, and an officer has asked to see your card. It is a routine stop and the card is in your wallet, which is where it has to be — a photograph of it on your phone does not count, and not having it is a fine. He looks at the status printed on the front and asks, conversationally, what you are here for.

line.en: I'm a student.

items.turn: です is not the verb "to be". It sits at the end and says: that was the statement, and I am making it politely. 学生です is nearer to "student — politely" than to a sentence with a verb in it, which is why it can stand alone with nothing in front of it.
claims: Police may ask foreign residents to produce their residence card, and failure to carry it is punishable by a fine of up to ¥200,000
A photocopy or a photograph on a phone does not satisfy the carrying requirement
Refusing to present the card carries a heavier penalty than failing to carry it
flags: How routine such stops are varies by area and is contested; the setting says 'a routine stop' without claiming a frequency.

items.why_this_lesson: The three-way split needs three things in three places, which a counter gives you for free: one document in front of you, one in front of the clerk, one somewhere else entirely.
items.setting: The counter at the city office. Three things are on it: the form you have just filled in, sitting in front of you; your residence card, which the clerk has slid to her side to copy the number from; and a rack of leaflets against the far wall that you will need one of before you leave. She asks which of them is yours to keep.

line.en: That one — by you — is the card.

items.turn: English splits pointing two ways; Japanese splits it three, and the middle one is measured from the listener rather than from you. Your own card becomes それ the moment it crosses the counter — the distance that matters is theirs, not the room's.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation, nothing to verify beyond the Japanese.

items.why_this_lesson: The drill is two choices at once — distance, then which set. A lost-property window forces both: you must point at one object among several, at a distance, without being able to name it.
items.setting: The station lost-property window, the morning after you left a bag on the train. The staff member has gone into the back and returned with three of them, which he sets on a shelf behind the counter, well out of reach of either of you. He does not ask you to describe it. He just waits for you to point.

line.en: That one — over there, away from both of us.

contrast.en: Same distance, but now holding a noun — あの cannot stand alone.

items.turn: Two decisions in one word, and your first language makes neither of them consciously. Distance first — near me, near you, or away from us both — then whether the word stands alone or leans on a noun. あれ本です is the error the two sets produce, and it is the commonest one in this step.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: Negation of a noun is most useful the moment somebody has written the wrong noun down about you — and on immigration paperwork the wrong noun is not a small thing.
items.setting: The clerk has been working from your visa category and has ticked a box that says student. You are not one; you are here to work, and the box governs which of two forms you will be filling in for the next twenty minutes. She is already reaching for the wrong one, and you have about four seconds to say so politely.

line.en: I'm not a student.

contrast.en: The same thing, one degree more formal — what you'll see in writing.

items.turn: This negative belongs to nouns and な-adjectives only. い-adjectives negate themselves — 高い becomes 高くない, never 高いじゃない — and the two systems get mixed constantly for a year. Learn this one as the noun negative and it stays out of the other's way.
claims: The status of residence printed on the card determines which procedures and forms apply

items.why_this_lesson: Past tense of です needs a state that has ended and mattered. Arriving at a government counter to find it shut is the version of that every new resident gets, usually once.
items.setting: You took the afternoon off, cycled twenty minutes, and found the shutters down. Public offices keep short weekday hours and close at weekends, so the errand you had to do inside fourteen days now has to happen inside eleven. Back at work the next morning, somebody asks whether you got it sorted out.

line.en: It was closed.

items.turn: です moved into the past, and it moves as one word rather than by changing anything in front of it. Same restriction as the negative: nouns and な-adjectives only. 寒いでした is wrong — い-adjectives carry their own past, 寒かったです, and that is a different machine.
claims: Municipal offices generally operate weekday daytime hours and close at weekends
The 14-day registration deadline runs regardless of whether the office was open
flags: Some municipalities run limited evening or Saturday counters; the setting does not claim otherwise, but a reviewer may want that softened further.

items.why_this_lesson: か costs one syllable and converts everything the learner can already say into a question. The setting should be one where asking is unavoidable and pointing is not enough.
items.setting: Four windows, four queues, and a numbered ticket in your hand that does not say which of them it belongs to. The signs above each one are in kanji you cannot read yet. Everybody in the room knows where they are going except you, and the only tool you have is a sentence you already know with one sound added to the end.

line.en: Is it this one?

items.turn: No word order changes and no verb moves. Japanese asks by adding か and letting the intonation stay flat, which means every statement you can already make is also a question you can already ask. That is an unusually large return for one syllable.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: The negative-question trap needs a moment where getting it backwards actually costs something. An immigration officer confirming your status is that moment — the answer goes on a form, and the form governs what you are allowed to do.
items.setting: The immigration office, renewing your status. The officer is reading from your file and checking one detail he already believes he knows. 「学生じゃないですか」 — you're not a student, are you? You are not. Your English instinct is about to answer the fact, and the fact is no, so the word arriving in your mouth is いいえ.

line.jp: はい、学生じゃないです。
line.en: That's right — I'm not a student.

contrast.en: Heard as: what you said is wrong — meaning you ARE one.

items.turn: はい agrees with the statement, not with the fact, so a negative question puts English and Japanese in opposite corners. The escape while the reflex builds is to drop the particle entirely and answer with the predicate — 学生じゃないです on its own is completely natural and cannot be misread.
claims: Negative questions are common in polite Japanese because they soften the asking
flags: The softening claim is the module's own teaching, carried over; it is linguistic judgement rather than a sourced fact and the reviewer should confirm it.

items.why_this_lesson: Question words are most vivid where you can see the thing you are asking about but cannot name it. A form in kanji, with a finger on one box, is the purest version.
items.setting: A form with eleven boxes, of which you have confidently filled in three. The clerk has stepped away. The man beside you is filling in the same form at speed, and you need to know what goes in the fourth box badly enough to interrupt him, with your finger on it so that the question has somewhere to land.

line.en: What is this?

items.turn: The question word sits exactly where the answer will sit — Japanese does not drag it to the front the way English does. Turn 田中さんが来ました into a question and only the name changes: 誰が来ましたか. Nothing else in the sentence moves at all.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: ね needs something both people can already see. A shared wait is the most reliable generator of that in the whole language, and the waiting room is where a new resident spends a surprising amount of the first month.
items.setting: Forty minutes into a numbered wait at the city office, on a row of plastic chairs, next to a woman who arrived before you did. Neither of you is going anywhere. She catches your eye and says something about the weather, and what she is doing is not conveying information — you are both sitting in the same room and you both already know.

line.en: Nice weather, isn't it.

items.turn: ね hands the thought across and asks the other person to nod. It only works on something already shared, which is why weather does so much of the work — it is the one topic guaranteed to be common ground. Announcing genuine news with ね sounds wrong, and that job belongs to よ.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: よ marks what the listener does not yet know, so the setting has to give the learner an information advantage — rare and satisfying this early, and it happens most often when somebody is about to make a mistake you have already made.
items.setting: The same waiting room, a week later. A man two seats along is holding the pale blue form, and you know from having got it wrong yourself last Tuesday that the counter he is queuing for wants the white one. He is about to stand up. You have one short sentence and no vocabulary for any of the nouns involved.

line.en: That's not the one, you know.

items.turn: よ flags the sentence as news: heads up, you did not know this. It earns its keep exactly here and turns pushy everywhere else — used on something the listener already knows, it lectures. When you are not sure whether they know, leave it off; a bare です is never rude.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: The three particles differ only in what each person already knows, so the drill needs one sentence said by two people in different states of knowledge. The same waiting room gives that without any new vocabulary.
items.setting: August, no air conditioning worth the name in the older part of the building, and an hour on the plastic chairs. The woman beside you has been there as long as you have. The clerk who comes out to call the next number has spent the morning behind a desk in the cooled office at the back, and says the same thing about the heat that everyone else has been saying.

line.en: Hot, isn't it — we both feel it.

contrast.en: Said to the clerk who has just come out: news, you haven't been in it.

items.turn: English does all of this with tone of voice, so nothing in your first language tells you which one you need. ね shares, よ informs, よね states a belief and asks for backup. The one that lands badly is よ about the listener's own experience — 疲れていますよ tells someone how tired they are.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: は sets a topic and then comments on it, so the setting wants a moment where the topic is obvious and has to be stated anyway — a form asking about you, in a room where everything is about you.
items.setting: The bank, opening an account, which needs the card and the address you registered a fortnight ago. The teller is working down a list of questions, and each one puts a different thing on the table: your address, your employer, your reason for opening it. Then she reaches the line about you, and pauses with the pen over it.

line.en: As for me — student.

items.turn: は is not "am" and it is not a subject marker. It puts something on the stage and everything after it is a comment on that thing; です does the stating. Two jobs, two words, and English collapses both into one verb — which is why 私は gets misread as "I am" for months.
claims: Opening a bank account generally requires a residence card and a registered address

items.why_this_lesson: が introduces something new, so the setting needs an arrival — someone or something entering the situation for the first time, which is precisely what が is for.
items.setting: Your number is called and you stand up, and so does somebody else — a friend has come along to help with the Japanese, and the clerk has not met them and does not know who they are. She looks between the two of you. What the sentence has to do is put a new person into the conversation who was not in it a second ago.

line.en: A friend came (with me).

items.turn: が points at which one, and its natural home is the first mention. It also answers who-questions, which is the same job seen from the other side: 誰が来ましたか and its answer both take が, because identifying the person is the entire point of the exchange.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: The handoff needs two consecutive sentences about one person — new, then known. A single introduction gives both halves in the order the lesson teaches them.
items.setting: The clerk has understood that somebody came with you, and now wants to know what they are to you, which is a second question about a person who has stopped being a surprise. The same human being is about to appear in two sentences in a row, and the particle changes between them for no reason English would recognise.

line.jp: 友達が来ました。友達は日本人です。
line.en: A friend came. The friend is Japanese.

items.turn: が put him on the table; は picked him up once he was on it. English marks the same difference with "a" and "the", and with stress — which is why translating either particle gives you nothing usable. The handoff between the two sentences is the pattern in miniature.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: を marks what an action lands on, so the setting only needs one deliberate action with one clear object. The morning of an appointment gives that without any vocabulary the learner does not have.
items.setting: The counter opens at half past eight and the queue starts before it. You have set an alarm for the first time since you arrived, and you are eating standing up, because the difference between arriving at 8:25 and arriving at 8:50 is about ninety minutes of your day. Everything in the sentence is ordinary; the particle is the whole lesson.

line.en: I eat breakfast.

items.turn: を tags the thing the action is done to, and it is written with a character that exists for nothing else. The trap is later and worth flagging now: not every English object takes it. 好き, ほしい and わかる all take が instead, which Step 10 drills specifically.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: The rule worth carrying out of this lesson is the exception — に does not attach to 今日 or 明日. So the setting should produce a sentence about today, where the particle the learner wants to add is the one that must not be there.
items.setting: You have been putting the ward office off for nine days and there are five left. Somebody at work asks when you are finally going to go, and the honest answer is the one you have been avoiding: not next week, not on some numbered day you could write down, but today, straight after this conversation.

line.en: I'm going today.

items.turn: に pins an action to a point you could write as a number — 七時に, 月曜日に. It does not attach to words that only mean something relative to now: 今日, 明日, 昨日, 毎日. 今日に行きます is wrong, and almost every English speaker makes it, because English says "on Monday" and "today" without noticing the difference.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.
No error-contrast shown: the design bans one in Steps 0-2, so the wrong form is named in the turn instead, where it cannot be mistaken for a model sentence.

items.why_this_lesson: Destination needs an actual journey with a purpose. A library card is the first thing most new residents get that is not compulsory, and getting one still needs the address they registered.
items.setting: Public libraries are free to anyone living in the area, and the card takes about ten minutes — you need proof that you live where you say you live, which is the same piece of paper everything else has wanted this month. It is the first errand of the fortnight that nobody is making you do, and the sentence for it is about going somewhere.

line.en: I'm going to the library.

contrast.en: The same journey, slightly softer and more directional.

items.turn: に and へ are interchangeable for travel, に being commoner in speech. What you must not reach for is で — that covers what you do once you have arrived, not the going. 図書館に行きます, and then 図書館で勉強します, and the next lesson but one puts the two side by side.
claims: Public library membership is generally free to residents of the municipality and requires proof of address
flags: UNSOURCED: library card requirements are municipal and vary. Stated loosely ('proof that you live where you say you live') for that reason, but a reviewer or a follow-up search should confirm before this ships.

items.why_this_lesson: This lesson is about typing as much as about reading — the module's own build beat is about what the IME expects. So the setting should be a keyboard, and a form that will not accept what you typed.
items.setting: An online application, in Japanese, that will not let you past the name field. You have switched the keyboard over and you are typing what you hear, which is how you have got わたしわ into the box twice. What is on the screen is not what the sentence sounds like, and the two have to be told apart before anything else will work.

line.jp: 私は図書館へ行きます。
line.en: Read: watashi wa toshokan e ikimasu — two spelling quirks in one short sentence.

items.turn: The special reading applies only when the kana is doing a particle's job: はな is hana, but the は in 私は is wa. Typing follows the spelling and not the sound — type 'ha' for the particle and 'wo' for を. Typing 'wa' gets you わ, which is the commonest input slip there is.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

The gloss contains romaji, which is normally banned outside the kana module. It is deliberate here: this lesson is ABOUT the sound-spelling mismatch and cannot be taught without naming both. Flagged so the romaji check reports it rather than silently normalising it.

items.why_this_lesson: で marks the stage an action happens on, so the setting wants a place chosen deliberately for the thing being done there — not somewhere you happen to be.
items.setting: Your apartment has one room and a wall you share with somebody who works nights. The park by the station has benches, and on Saturday mornings a man practises a wind instrument at the far end of it, which somehow makes it easier rather than harder. You have arranged to meet the friend who came to the ward office with you.

line.jp: 公園で友達に会いました。
line.en: I met a friend at the park.

items.turn: で needs a real action to mark. Simply being somewhere is not one — that is に with あります and います, two lessons from now. The test is whether anything is happening: if it is, the place takes で.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: Same particle, different job, and the everyday version of the second job is transport. A new resident without a registered bicycle or a car takes the train to everything, so the instrument is real rather than illustrative.
items.setting: The ward office is two stations away. You do not have a car — that would mean proving to the police you have somewhere off-street to keep it — and the bicycle you were given by a departing colleague is still not registered in your name. So every errand this month has started on the same platform, and the sentence for it marks the train as a tool.

line.en: I'll go by train.

items.turn: Same で, marking the instrument now rather than the stage — vehicle, language, material, tool. The one it is not for is people: a person you did something with takes と. 友達で行きます would suggest you used your friend to travel in.
claims: Registering a car requires a police-issued parking certificate (車庫証明) under the 1962 Garage Act
flags: Bicycle registration (防犯登録) is mentioned in passing and is not sourced here; it is near-universal in practice but the requirement is prefectural.

items.why_this_lesson: The split is not about the place, it is about the verb — so the setting must keep the building fixed and change only what is happening in it. The library, twice.
items.setting: The library card worked. You are in there on a Sunday for the second time, and you want to say two things about the same building: that you come here to work, and that the thing you are looking for is somewhere on the second floor. The room does not change between those two sentences. The particle does.

line.jp: 図書館に本があります。
line.en: There are books in the library. — existence

contrast.en: I study at the library. — action

items.turn: Ask one question before choosing and it comes out right every time: is something happening here, or is something simply located here? Happening takes で, located takes に. Both sentences above are correct about the same building — the verb decided, not the room.
flags: No factual claims — an ordinary situation.

items.why_this_lesson: NATURAL MERGE. The scene invented a rural station at night with no cash; the anecdote had already established with a METI figure why that situation is real rather than picturesque. Neither half knew about the other.
items.setting: The last bus has gone. There is a taxi rank with no taxi on it and one shop still lit. Japan is going cashless slowly — 42.8% of consumer spending in 2024, against a government target of 80% — and out here that average means nothing: the shop takes cash, the taxi firm takes cash, and you are counting what is in your wallet before you go in.

line.en: I've only got a thousand yen.

items.turn: しか forces the verb negative and the sentence still means you have money — just not enough of it. English "only" sits happily beside a positive verb, which is why the reflex to reach for だけ outlives the rule. だけ counts what is there; しか complains about it.
claims: Cashless payments reached 42.8% of consumer spending in 2024 (METI)
Japan's long-term cashless target is 80%, with 65% by 2030
Cash acceptance remains the norm in rural businesses and small operators
flags: The rural cash-only detail is resident experience rather than a sourced statistic; the national figure is sourced, the local inference is not.

items.why_this_lesson: REWRITTEN ON LLOYD'S NOTE — the medicine-booklet version was relatable but optional, and the register that fits a learner's life is the required kind. Carrying the residence card is not a habit, it is the law, and 持っていく／持ってくる is exactly the pair a counter clerk uses about it. Also the clearest case of the spec's principle: 'always have it on you' READS like obligation grammar and maps mechanically to なければなりません, but what anybody actually says is a verb about carrying, pointed in a direction.
items.setting: You have come to collect the new card and the clerk is explaining what happens next. Over sixteen and staying more than three months, you must have it on you every day — not a photocopy, not a photograph on your phone, the card itself, with a fine of up to two hundred thousand yen if an officer asks and you cannot produce it. She slides it across and tells you what to do with it.

line.jp: カードを持っていってください。
line.en: Take the card with you — away from here, from now on.

contrast.jp: カードを持ってきてください。
contrast.en: Bring the card with you — said about coming back next time.

items.turn: Same card, two verbs, and the only difference is where the speaker is standing. English uses "bring" and "take" for this and confuses them constantly; Japanese hangs it on 来る and 行く, which is why 行ってきます — off I go and I'll be back — has been this pattern since your first week.
claims: Mid-to-long-term residents aged 16 and over must carry the residence card at all times
The card is issued to foreign nationals staying more than three months
A photocopy or phone photograph does not satisfy the requirement
Failure to carry it is punishable by a fine of up to ¥200,000; refusing to present it carries up to one year's imprisonment or the same fine
flags: Short-term visitors, diplomats and special permanent residents are outside this rule and carry other documents; the setting states the conditions (over 16, staying over three months) rather than generalising to every foreigner.
Whether a clerk would phrase it as 持っていってください rather than 持ち歩いてください is the reviewer's third question.

items.why_this_lesson: FACT-LED. There was no scene here — the fact came first and produced the situation. なら is the topical if: it picks up what the other person has just raised and hangs advice on it, which is exactly what someone does when you mention which city you are moving to.
items.setting: You are moving west and you mention it in the staffroom, and someone asks what you are taking with you. Japan runs on two mains frequencies — Tokyo and everything east of it on 50 Hz, Osaka and everything west on 60 Hz — because in the 1890s the Tokyo company bought German generators and the Osaka company bought American ones, and nobody ever unified them. Most modern appliances cope. Yours is fifteen years old.

line.jp: 大阪なら、その電子レンジは使えません。
line.en: If it's Osaka — that microwave won't work.

contrast.jp: 大阪に行くと、その電子レンジは使えません。
contrast.en: と claims it happens automatically on arrival, as if the journey broke it.

items.turn: なら takes what the other person just said and makes it the topic: if Osaka is what we're discussing, here is what follows. It is also the only one of the four ifs that can advise about before the condition — the pattern for reacting to a plan rather than stating a rule.
claims: Eastern Honshu and Hokkaido run at 50 Hz; western Honshu, Kyushu, Shikoku and Okinawa at 60 Hz
Tokyo Electric Light bought 50 Hz AEG generators around 1895-96; Osaka Electric Light bought 60 Hz generators from GE's predecessor shortly after
No regulation required a single frequency at the time, and later unification was judged too costly
Some older motor-driven and clock appliances are frequency-dependent; most modern equipment is not
flags: Which specific appliances still fail across the line is stated loosely on purpose — the sourced claim is the split and its history, not an appliance list.
大阪 uses 阪, outside KANJI_DICT — furigana decision needed.

items.step: Step 20 · Doing to & being done to
items.why_this_lesson: NATURAL MERGE, and it carries a myth correction. The scene had invented 毎日そうじをさせられました for a story about a first year at a company. The anecdote was about 掃除の時間 sitting in the national curriculum. They were the same lesson, written twice, from opposite ends of the folder.
items.setting: Half past one, and your class is cleaning the corridor they walk down every day — brooms, cloths, fifteen minutes of it, in the timetable rather than beside it. You say something about it to the teacher next to you, who is old enough to have done it himself for twelve years, and he laughs before he answers.

line.jp: 毎日、そうじをさせられました。
line.en: I was made to do the cleaning every day.

contrast.jp: 毎日、そうじをしました。
contrast.en: Grammatical, and it drops the whole point — that nobody asked him.

items.turn: Causative first, passive second, and the grudge rides along inside the ending — English needs "was made to" plus a tone of voice to do the same work. Build it in two moves every time; jumping straight to させられる is where the longest conjugation in the language breaks.
claims: A daily cleaning slot of roughly 15-30 minutes, usually after lunch, is standard in Japanese schools
Cleaning appears in the national curriculum standards (学習指導要領), not as an extracurricular add-on
